findings.description: The timeout_ms check uses a truthy ternary (`input.timeout_ms ? ... : {}`). When timeout_ms is 0, the condition is falsy and no timeout limit is set, silently converting an explicit 0ms timeout request into an infinite timeout. This could cause indefinite hangs in production if a caller passes 0. Negative values are also passed through unvalidated to execSandboxed.

The cwd parameter is passed directly to execSandboxed without any validation in this wrapper. Path traversal protection depends entirely on the unseen sandbox implementation. If the sandbox profile does not constrain cwd to allowed directories, a caller could execute commands in arbitrary filesystem locations.

No try/catch around execSandboxed. If the sandbox throws, the raw error (potentially containing paths, argv, or system details) propagates unmodified to the caller. Acceptable for a library function if the caller sanitizes, but worth noting since command-execution errors may include sensitive context.

independent_verifier.summary: This is a thin wrapper that delegates to execSandboxed. It uses safe patterns—argv passed as an array (avoiding shell injection), no dynamic object key construction (no prototype pollution risk), and no regex (no ReDoS). The primary concerns are minor: the truthy check on timeout_ms silently drops a 0 value (potential indefinite hang), and all security guarantees (path traversal for cwd, shell execution mode for argv) depend on the unseen execSandboxed implementation. No critical vulnerabilities are present in this file itself.
